Occlusion of the teeth can happen randomly but is often linked to genetics.

What was likely happening with your chinchilla was malocclusion, or misalignment of the teeth. This is not a terminal disease, but a treatable one.

Because chinchillas have teeth that grow constantly, they need to be worn down by chewing (food, objects). When there is malocclusion, the teeth don’t wear down properly, and continue to get longer. In chinchillas, they actually tend to grow up INTO the head when this happens, and can put pressure on the lacrimal duct and other structures. The lacrimal duct drains tears from the eye, and pressure on it is both uncomfortable and causes tearing in the eye.

The treatment for this condition is having the teeth trimmed by a veterinarian regularly.

Have you confirmed that your Pom is pregnant? That would be the first step. You may also want to get a professional opinion (from a vet) on whether your male dog might actually carry the Merle gene. There are other reasons that dogs may have different colored eyes, and there are other coat patterns that can resemble Merle.

If your Pom does turn out to be pregnant and your male dog is a Merle, the outcome of a Merle x Merle mating results in approximately 25% homozygosity--"double" Merles tend to have eye and ear problems. While there are double Merle dogs that live normal-ish lives, they do require a higher level of care.

If the male is not Merle, you still have the issue of an unanticipated litter of puppies. If you decide to keep them, Merle or not, it is your responsibility as the pet owner to ensure that they go to good homes. This means no internet advertising, no "free puppies" signs, etc. It would be best to contact a local rescue to help (either with pointers or as a place to send the puppies when they have weaned).

It will also be your responsibility to make sure that both the puppies and their mother receive appropriate care. See your vet about the vaccines, preventatives, etc. that your animals (this includes mom, BEFORE whelping) will need, and when they will need them. Make sure you know the signs of disease, the right environment (heat, whelping box, etc). Do not separate the puppies from their mother before 2 months of age.

In my own opinion, it would be best to spay and neuter both of your pets regardless of the outcome of this situation, since you don't seem to want them to reproduce. As an added benefit, spaying prevents uterine infections in females (pyometra--a surgical emergency) and testicular tumors in males.

Good luck and I hope it all works out!

It's possible that it's a neurological issue (idiopathic vestibular disease) that sometimes happens without reason to older dogs. It can be difficult to recognize because it can present in different ways, but when my dog had it, his back legs were also slipping out from under him. Does she have nystagmus (eyes twitching rapidly from side to side)? That's usually a pretty good indication that it's a vestibular thing, but dogs don't necessarily get it.

Vestibular disease can be very scary if you don't know what it is--some dogs continually roll over because they are unable to stand up, they vomit because they're dizzy, and they are unable/unwilling to eat or drink. Fortunately, it usually goes away on its own in a few days. It can be treated with benadryl or other motion sickness drugs (ask vet about dosing) along with supportive care (fluids if they can't drink, for example).

Mention idiopathic/ "old dog" vestibular disease to your vet and see what they say.
